notes.w: Everything that changes the switch starts here. The prompt grows (config) and stays until you type end. Unique abbreviations work: conf t is the same thing.
notes.tip: Take a checkpoint before a change you might want to undo: copy running-config checkpoint before-change.

notes.w: Leaves whatever context you are in and drops you at the exec prompt. exit goes up one level; end goes all the way.
Sets the name in the prompt, in LLDP and in logs. Letters, digits, dots and dashes, no spaces.
notes.tip: Put the location in the name. You will read it in an LLDP table at 2 a.m. someday.

notes.w: Copies the running configuration to the startup configuration so it survives a reboot. copy running-config startup-config does the same.
notes.tip: Save after the change is proven, not before. Until then a reboot is your rollback.

notes.w: The whole active configuration. Add interface 1/1/5 to see one port's block. Pipe it to cut it down: | begin, | include.
v: 10.16 added server priority lines and the built-in radius group to the output; 10.15 printed neither.

notes.w: The saved configuration, the one a reboot loads. If it differs from the running config, something has not been saved yet, on purpose or not.
The AOS-CX release and build. The first two letters say the platform: ML for the 6200, FL for the 6300. The release picker in the sandbox changes what this says.
Product name and part number, serial, base MAC, uptime and CPU. The part number is how you tell a 6200F 12-port from a 24-port when nobody wrote it down.
v: 10.18 added CPU idle, user and system lines; 10.17 printed CPU utilisation only.

notes.w: Turns off paging for this session, so long output scrolls instead of stopping every screen. Every script and screen capture should start with it.
Saves the running config under a name. If the running config is identical to a checkpoint that exists, 10.18 refuses with An identical checkpoint already exists.
notes.tip: The box also makes system checkpoints (CPC...) after changes on its own. Name yours so you can find them.

notes.w: Replaces the running config with the checkpoint. It does not ask. checkpoint diff checkpoint <name> running-config shows the difference first, and that is worth doing.
Every checkpoint, newest first, with the startup config among them by date. show checkpoint <name> prints one. There is no show checkpoint list on 10.18: the box reads list as a checkpoint name.

Compares any two of running-config, startup-config and checkpoint <name> as a unified diff: a line starting with a plus is only in the second, one starting with a minus only in the first. No difference in configs. means they match. Worth running before every rollback.
notes.tip: checkpoint diff startup-config running-config before you walk away tells you whether anything is unsaved.

notes.w: Creates the VLAN and enters its context. Name it there. A port cannot use a VLAN that does not exist.
Shows in show vlan and in LLDP. One word here; the box takes a longer line too.
Tells LLDP-MED this VLAN carries voice. Phones that speak LLDP-MED learn it from the network policy the switch sends on ports that tag it: VLAN, priority 6, DSCP 46 with nothing else configured.
notes.tip: Tag the voice VLAN on the phone port and leave the data VLAN native, so the PC behind the phone needs nothing.

notes.w: Every VLAN, up or down, and which ports carry it. Down with no_member_port means no port is in it; no_member_forwarding means ports are in it but none is up. A role a client holds adds its VLANs to that port here.

notes.t: Configure a port or a range
notes.w: Enters one port (1/1/5) or a range (1/1/1-1/1/8). Member/slot/port: 1/1/5 is member 1, slot 1, port 5.
Admin down. no shutdown turns it back on and also clears an error-disabled port. A port nobody configured may be shut: show interface brief says Administratively down.

notes.t: Say what is on the port
notes.w: Free text on the port, shown in show interface brief and LLDP.
ex: description desk 7, pair 3-6 open at 23 m
notes.tip: Describe uplinks and anything odd. The next person reads the brief, not your ticket.

notes.w: A routed port takes an ip address; a switched port takes VLANs. no routing makes it switched. Some platforms (and the Switch Simulator) start every port routed, so check before you assign a VLAN.
Makes the port an access port in that VLAN. The VLAN has to exist.
Makes the port a trunk and adds VLANs to its allowed list. It adds: vlan trunk allowed 10 then vlan trunk allowed 20 leaves 10,20, as the lab switch did. no vlan trunk allowed 10 takes one out.
notes.tip: A trunk prints vlan trunk native 1 even when you never set it. Set the native VLAN on purpose.

notes.t: The untagged VLAN on a trunk
notes.w: The VLAN whose frames cross the trunk untagged. On a phone port it is the PC's data VLAN; the phone tags voice.
speed auto offers every speed the port can do; speed auto 1g 2.5g offers only those; speed 1000-full fixes it and turns auto-negotiation off. Since 10.09 the CLI hides speeds the hardware lacks.
notes.fake: The sandbox models the hardware. The Switch Simulator has virtual ports and hides speed entirely; the syntax is from HPE's fundamentals guide.
notes.tip: Leave Smart Rate ports on speed auto. Pinning an AP to 1G to fix a flap hides the real problem, usually the cable.

notes.w: Native VLAN, mode, enabled, up or down, why it is down, speed and description. Read the Reason column first.
State, why it is down (State information), VLANs and counters. Blocked by Port Access Security means the link is up but no client has authenticated.
v: 10.15 says how long the link has been up; 10.16 says up; 10.17 added the Hardware port line.

notes.w: Link and admin state, the speed it runs at next to what it is configured to allow, flow control, PoE draw.
notes.fake: The PoE column is the sandbox's: the lab's virtual ports draw nothing.

notes.w: Learned MACs by VLAN and port. port-access-security means the MAC was learned through port-access. Filter by vlan or interface, or pipe it.
Creates lagN and enters it. On 10.18 a new LAG is administratively down: nothing forms until no shutdown.
notes.tip: Configure the LAG first, then put ports in it. Settings live on the LAG, not the members.

notes.t: Put a port in a LAG
notes.w: Makes the port a member. Its VLAN settings come from the LAG from then on.
active sends LACPDUs; passive only answers. Two passive ends never form a LAG. Without lacp mode the LAG is static: no LACP at all.
Asks the partner for a short timeout: a dead link is noticed in about three seconds instead of ninety. The S in PSFNCD is the partner asking for the same.
Actor and partner state per member. ALFNCD is what you want: Active, Long timeout, aggregable, in sync, collecting, distributing. An empty partner line means nothing is talking back.
v: 10.18 added IE (LACP fallback active) to the legend; 10.17 has no such line.

notes.t: Each LAG, its members and mode
notes.w: Members, heartbeat rate, hash and mode per LAG.
MSTP by default. Without it an accidental loop takes the VLAN down. mode rpvst switches to Rapid PVST+.
notes.tip: Decide who is root and set their priority low. Leave it to chance and the oldest switch wins.

notes.w: A port where only end devices live: it forwards at once instead of waiting through listening and learning.

notes.t: Shut the port if a switch appears
notes.w: A BPDU arriving on the port error-disables it. Pair it with admin-edge on every access port. no shutdown brings it back once the switch is gone.
notes.tip: Access ports: admin-edge plus bpdu-guard. Uplinks: neither.

notes.t: Catch loops spanning tree cannot see
notes.w: Sends probes and error-disables the port if one comes back, which catches a loop through an unmanaged switch that drops BPDUs.

notes.t: Root, role and state per port
notes.w: Who is root, which port leads there, and each port's role and state.

notes.t: Send voice VLAN policy to phones
notes.w: On by default. On a port that tags a voice VLAN the switch sends LLDP-MED network policy, but only after it has heard the endpoint's own LLDP-MED TLVs. no lldp med network-policy stops it.
v: New in 10.18: lldp med force-send. By default MED TLVs go out only after the endpoint's own arrive (HPE's guide and the lab agree); the sandbox does not model force-send.

notes.w: LLDP sends and listens on every port by default. no lldp transmit and no lldp receive turn each half off.
The LLDP table: port, chassis, remote port, name. Give a port for the full record: capabilities, power it asks for, LLDP-MED class and network policy.
notes.tip: On a port-access port the switch drops LLDP from a client that has not authenticated, unless the port has allow-lldp-bpdu. An empty neighbour on a phone port is often that.

notes.w: Defines a RADIUS server and the shared secret. The running config shows the key as ciphertext. A wrong key looks like a dead server: the server drops the request and the switch times out.
ex: radius-server host 192.0.2.11 key plaintext cppm-lab-key vrf mgmt
notes.tip: Use a group (aaa group server radius) even with one server, so adding the second is one line.

notes.w: Port-access points at a group, not a server. Servers are tried in priority order; entered without a priority they number themselves in the order you add them.
v: 10.16 added server <ip> priority <n>; 10.15 has no priority in a group.
10.18 added load-balancing-mode (round-robin or priority-based) in the group.

notes.w: Each server with its ports and VRF. A star in front means the switch has marked it unreachable.
Counters per server. Timeouts climbing with no accepts usually means the shared secret. show radius-server statistics on its own is incomplete on 10.18.
ex: show radius-server statistics authentication | include Timeouts

notes.w: Lets ClearPass change or end a session after the fact (RFC 5176). On 10.18 that is two pieces: enable it, and name each server allowed to send with radius dyn-authorization client. Without the client line requests are dropped and counted as invalid client addresses.
ex: radius dyn-authorization client 192.0.2.10 secret-key plaintext cppm-lab-key

notes.w: Whether dynamic authorization is on, the port (3799), the invalid-address counters, and per client the CoA and disconnect requests, ACKs and NAKs.
Global switch for 802.1X plus the RADIUS group it uses. It needs enable here and on each port: either one off and nothing authenticates.
The same pattern as 802.1X: a global block with the group and enable, and enable per port. The switch sends the MAC as username and password, 00005e005305 style by default.

notes.t: How many clients a port takes
notes.w: One by default. A PC behind a phone needs two, or a multi-domain port. Only clients that got in take a place.
v: 10.18 added client-limit device-mode <n> on the port and in a role.

notes.w: dot1x then mac-auth is the default. A device with no supplicant waits out the 802.1X timeout before MAC auth starts; mac-auth first is faster for printers and slower for laptops.
ex: aaa authentication port-access auth-precedence mac-auth dot1x
aaa authentication port-access auth-precedence dot1x mac-auth

notes.t: A role when RADIUS is down
notes.w: If every RADIUS server times out, clients get this role instead of nothing. reject-role is the same for a reject.
notes.tip: Decide what a building does when ClearPass is unreachable before it happens. Critical role is that decision written down.

notes.t: A phone and a PC on one port
notes.w: One voice device and one data device (client-limit multi-domain raises the data count). The voice device is whoever holds a role with device-traffic-class voice.

A port-access port drops LLDP from a client that has not authenticated. A phone that never authenticates is then invisible to LLDP, its device profile never matches, and it gets no voice VLAN. This lets LLDP through. Found the hard way on the lab switch on 2026-09-28.
v: 10.17 added aaa authentication port-access lldp-loop-guard enable beside it.

notes.w: What a client gets once it is in: an access VLAN, or a native VLAN and a tagged list, and more on 10.18. RADIUS names the role; the switch must have it or the client fails authorization.
v: 10.18 added speed, voice-vlan, stp-bpdu-guard, rate-limits, toggle-link and client-limit device-mode to a role.

notes.t: This role is the voice device
notes.w: On a multi-domain port the client holding this role is the voice device. Pair it with a native data VLAN and the voice VLAN tagged.

Clients in this role are tunnelled to the gateway cluster of the zone, where the gateway role applies. That is user-based tunnelling when RADIUS assigns the role, port-based when a port's fallback role does.

One line per client: port, name, role, VLAN, and four flags: how it got in (1x, ma, dp), mode (c, d, m), device type (d, v) and status (s, f, p). --|c|-|f is a failure. Add detail for the history, interface, mac or role to filter.
notes.tip: Read Auth History in the detail view bottom to top: it is the order things happened.

notes.k: show aaa authentication port-access interface all client-status
notes.w: The authentication and authorization blocks for every client, without VLAN and MACsec detail.
ex: show aaa authentication port-access interface all client-status
show aaa authentication port-access interface 1/1/1 client-status

notes.t: The roles and what they carry
notes.w: Each local role: VLANs, device type, gateway zone. show port-access role name X for one.
10.18 has no clear port-access clients. To start clients over: reauthenticate a port, or log one off by MAC, port or role.

notes.t: Recognise a device by its LLDP
notes.w: Ordered match and ignore rules; the first rule a neighbour hits decides. sysname is exact, sys-desc matches if the description contains the word (proved on the lab switch), vendor-oui plus type matches a TLV. Rules without seq number themselves 10, 20, 30.
v: 10.18 added match chassis-id. sys-desc, sysname and vendor-oui are there from 10.15.

notes.t: Give a recognised device a role
notes.w: Ties an LLDP group to a role, then enable. Works on a port with no port-access at all; on a port-access port it applies when 802.1X and MAC auth do not get the device in. The client shows as dp.
The profiles and their state. interface all lists each matched neighbour with its profile, group, role and whether it applied.

notes.t: A role for whatever is on the port
notes.w: The role a client gets when nothing else gives it one. With no authentication on the port that is everything plugged in: with a gateway zone in the role, that is port-based tunnelling.
In local-vlan mode (what show ubt reports) this is the reserved VLAN all tunnelled client traffic uses to reach the gateway. Create it first and use it for nothing else, as HPE's guide says.
A zone names the gateway cluster: primary and backup controller addresses, reached in a VRF, and enable. show ubt says whether it is up.
notes.fake: The gateway is a bench device in the sandbox; a zone is up when the switch can reach it.

notes.w: Each zone's controllers, VLAN, admin and operational state. brief is one line per zone; users all lists who is tunnelled.
A switch virtual interface: the switch's own address in that VLAN, up only when a port in the VLAN is up.
Prefix and next hop. The default route is 0.0.0.0/0.
The process, its router-id and areas. Interfaces join with ip ospf <process> area <area>. Both ends of a link must agree on the area.
Connected (C), local (L), static (S) and OSPF (O) routes with next hop and interface.

Virtual Switching Framework: pre-provision a member by part number and name the ports that form its stack links. A member's links are its own ports, 2/1/x for member 2. Member 1 is the switch you are on. vsf secondary-member picks the standby; without it there is none.
notes.fake: The Switch Simulator has no VSF, so nothing here was checked against a capture. The syntax is from HPE's VSF guide; the sandbox never cables a second switch.

notes.w: Each member with its role (conductor, standby, member), status and part number. show vsf link lists the stack links and whether they are up.
notes.fake: The layout is the sandbox's own: the Switch Simulator has no VSF to capture. A provisioned member shows Not Present because no second switch is ever cabled.

notes.w: Writes port-access events to the debug buffer, the default destination. debug radius all and debug lldp event add those modules. show debug lists what is on; no debug all turns it off.
ex: show debug buffer module lldp | include 1/1/6
notes.tip: Clear the buffer, turn debug on, reproduce once, read, turn it off. A busy switch fills the buffer in seconds.

notes.w: Everything logged, oldest first. module portaccess, radius or lldp narrows it; a pipe narrows it further.
ex: show debug buffer module portaccess | include DEVICEPROFILE
notes.fake: The sandbox logs the lines that tell a client's story, in the lab's format; the box logs far more.

notes.t: Test the cable from the switch
notes.w: A TDR test on a copper port: per pair good, open or short, the cable length or the distance to the fault. It drops the link while it runs and asks first. show prints the result; clear forgets it.
notes.fake: Faked hardware. The Switch Simulator has no PHY and refuses the command; the sandbox builds the result from the lab's description of the cable, in the guide's layout.

notes.w: sim rest is a laptop calling the REST API: log in, then GET, POST, PATCH or DELETE under /rest/v10.18, and POST /rest/v10.18/cli for AnyCLI, which runs only the exact commands GET /rest/v10.18/cli/commands lists. Each answer names its CLI twin.
notes.fake: A sandbox command, not a switch command: the shapes are the lab switch's REST answers from 2026-09-28.

notes.w: The sandbox talking, not the switch. sim connect and sim disconnect plug bench devices in and out, sim coa has the fake ClearPass send a change of authorization, sim release picks the AOS-CX release, sim status shows what is plugged in.
